opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually a really useful analogy, and it's one I come back to a lot.

If you think about how self-driving matured, a big part of it was realizing you can't just put cars on real roads and wait for the rare, dangerous situations to happen. You need simulation. You build a virtual world where you can replay a near-miss a thousand times, vary the weather, vary what the pedestrian does, and see how your system responds before anyone gets hurt. The simulator becomes the place where you test, stress, and iterate cheaply.

I see simulations of people playing a similar role for decisions that involve human behavior. If you're designing a policy, launching a product, or building a social platform, today you mostly find out how people react after you've deployed it, when the consequences are already real and sometimes hard to undo. With generative agents grounded in rich data about real individuals, like the interview-based agents we've built, you can ask "what if" questions first. How would this community respond to this intervention? How might this feature change the way people interact online? You get a sandbox for the social world, the way driving simulators are a sandbox for the physical one.

But the analogy also teaches some humility. Self-driving simulators are only as useful as their fidelity, and the hard part was always the long tail, the weird edge cases the simulator didn't capture. Same for us. People are far more complex than traffic, and if a simulation only reproduces the average, stereotypical person, it can mislead you in exactly the cases that matter most. So much of our work is about measuring how accurate these agents actually are, benchmarking them against how real people answer surveys or behave in experiments, and being clear about where they break down.

And there's one big difference: in driving, the simulated pedestrian doesn't have a stake in how the simulation is used. With people, it does. These are representations of real individuals, so consent, privacy, and how the agents are deployed all matter in a way they don't for a virtual intersection. The engineering lesson transfers well. The ethical one we have to think through more carefully ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses testing varied and rare scenarios in simulation, but does not identify generalization beyond training data as a shared objective.

r002.rationale: It mentions agents grounded in rich data about real individuals, but does not say that learning from them captures aspects that cannot be explicitly programmed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the analogy is actually pretty deep, and it's one I come back to a lot.

When people were first building self-driving systems, there was this realization that you can't just collect enough real-world driving data to cover every situation a car will encounter. The long tail is enormous. So simulation became central. You build a simulated environment where you can run millions of scenarios, including the dangerous and rare ones you'd never want to test on a real street, and you use that to train and evaluate the system before it ever touches the road.

I think the parallel for simulations of people is that we're trying to do something similar for the social world. If you want to understand how a policy will land, or how a community will respond to a new product, or how misinformation might spread, you can't just run those experiments on real populations at scale. It's expensive, it's slow, and in many cases it's unethical. So the question becomes whether you can build a simulation of human behavior that's faithful enough that you can test ideas there first.

Where the analogy starts to strain is in what "faithful" means. In driving, the physics is relatively well specified. You know how a car accelerates, how friction works, roughly how a pedestrian moves. With people, the underlying dynamics are far messier. A person's behavior depends on their history, their beliefs, their mood, the specific social context. So the hard part isn't rendering the environment, it's capturing the agent itself. That's really where the generative agents work comes from. The idea that a language model, given the right memory and reflection architecture, might act as a plausible stand-in for a specific person or a type of person.

The other thing I'd say is that both fields have to be honest about the gap between simulation and reality. A self-driving stack that works beautifully in simulation can still fail when a real sensor gets dirty. Likewise, a social simulation can produce very convincing-looking behavior that doesn't actually predict what real people do. So in both cases the real work is validation. You have to keep going back to the real world, measuring where the simulation diverges, and improving it from there. Simulation is a tool for exploring the space, not a replacement for ground truth.

r001.rationale: The response says real driving data cannot cover every situation, describes simulation as a way to explore rare scenarios, and presents the same need to test social-world situations in human simulations.

r002.rationale: It mentions people’s histories and beliefs and proposes language models with memory and reflection, but does not say that learning from real people captures aspects that cannot be explicitly programmed.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy is useful because, in both cases, simulation gives us a way to explore what might happen before we act in the real world. With a self-driving vehicle, you want to test how it behaves across different road conditions and situations without putting people at risk. With simulations of people, the question is whether we can give ourselves a similar space to test ideas about social systems—say, a different design for an online community or a policy intervention.

But there’s an important difference: people don’t have the same stable dynamics as physical objects. We interpret situations, adapt to one another, and change our behavior. So a simulation that produces something plausible isn’t necessarily predicting what real people would do. You need to validate it against human behavior for the particular question you’re asking.

The promise, to me, is a tool that helps us form better hypotheses and anticipate possible consequences before going out and testing those ideas with real people.

r001.rationale: The response says simulations can explore varied situations before real-world action, but it does not identify generalization beyond training data as a shared objective.

r002.rationale: The response calls for validating simulations against human behavior, but does not describe learning from real people to capture aspects of them that cannot be explicitly programmed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is useful because, with self-driving cars, you don’t want the first time a system encounters a difficult situation to be out on the road. You want a simulation where you can test different scenarios, understand what goes wrong, and improve the system before deploying it.

We could imagine something similar for systems that affect people. If you’re designing a new social platform or considering a policy, could you first explore how people might respond in a simulated environment?

But the important caveat is that people aren’t vehicles. Our behavior depends on context, relationships, and how we interpret what’s happening. So the goal shouldn’t be to claim that we can predict everyone perfectly. It’s to build a useful model, validate it against real human behavior, and understand where its predictions are trustworthy. Simulation can help us ask better questions before we run experiments in the real world.
